content: Granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF) and granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF) are naturally occurring cytokines that play a critical role in stimulating the production and enhancing the antibacterial functions of neutrophils and monocytes. These cytokines have been explored in neonatal medicine through two primary strategies. The first involves their use as a treatment for preterm infants with established systemic infections, particularly in cases complicated by low neutrophil counts. The second strategy involves their prophylactic use to prevent sepsis by stimulating neutrophil production and bactericidal activity in high-risk neonates. The objective of this review was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of G-CSF and GM-CSF in newborns for two specific purposes: (a) as a treatment for suspected or confirmed systemic infections to reduce mortality, and (b) as a prophylactic intervention to prevent systemic infections in neonates at high risk of nosocomial infections. Additionally, subgroup analyses were conducted to assess the impact of pre-existing or high-risk neutropenia on therapeutic outcomes. A comprehensive search of PubMed, EMBASE, MEDLINE, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials was conducted in April 2003. The search included terms such as G-CSF, GM-CSF, and infant newborn, with and without the Clinical Trial filter. Reference lists of identified randomized controlled trials (RCTs), meta-analyses, and personal files were also reviewed. Studies were included if they met the following criteria: (1) RCT design, (2) subjects were newborns in intensive care, (3) interventions involved G-CSF or GM-CSF as either treatment (in conjunction with antibiotics for suspected or confirmed systemic infections) or prophylaxis (to reduce the incidence of systemic infections), and (4) outcomes included all-cause mortality for treatment studies or the incidence of sepsis and/or mortality for prophylaxis studies. Data analysis involved calculating relative risks (RR) and risk differences (RD) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) using a fixed-effect model. The number needed to treat (NNT) was determined for outcomes showing statistically significant reductions in RR. Seven treatment studies involving 257 infants with suspected systemic bacterial infections and three prophylaxis studies involving 359 neonates were analyzed. In treatment studies, the addition of G-CSF or GM-CSF to antibiotic therapy in preterm infants with suspected systemic infections did not demonstrate a reduction in immediate all-cause mortality. No significant survival benefit was observed at 14 days post-therapy initiation (typical RR 0.71, 95% CI 0.38–1.33; typical RD -0.05, 95% CI -0.14–0.04). However, these studies were small, with the largest enrolling only 60 infants. A subgroup analysis of 97 infants from three treatment studies who had both systemic infections and clinically significant neutropenia (neutrophil count < 1.7 x 10^9/L) at trial entry showed a significant reduction in mortality by day 14 (RR 0.34, 95% CI 0.12–0.92; RD -0.18, 95% CI -0.33 to -0.03; NNT 6, 95% CI 3–33). Prophylaxis studies did not demonstrate a significant reduction in mortality among neonates receiving GM-CSF (RR 0.59, 95% CI 0.24–1.44; RD -0.03, 95% CI -0.08–0.02). The ability to identify sepsis as the primary outcome in these studies was limited by inconsistent and inadequately stringent definitions of systemic infection. However, data from one study suggested that prophylactic GM-CSF might offer protection against infection in preterm infants who are neutropenic or at high risk of developing postnatal neutropenia. The authors concluded that there is currently insufficient evidence to support the routine use of G-CSF or GM-CSF in neonatal practice, either as a treatment for established systemic infections to reduce mortality or as a prophylactic measure to prevent systemic infections in high-risk neonates. No toxicity related to CSF use was reported in any of the included studies. The limited evidence suggesting that CSF treatment may reduce mortality in cases of systemic infection accompanied by severe neutropenia warrants further investigation through adequately powered trials involving sufficient numbers of infants infected with organisms associated with significant mortality risks.
